dedupe_keys.name: air pollution from warehousing in the united states seen with satellite no2 data

description: This study by Gaige Hunter Kerr, Michelle Meyer, Daniel Goldberg, Joshua Miller and Susan Anenberg of George Washington University and the International Council on Clean Transportation (Nature Communications, 2024) uses nationwide data on warehouse locations, traffic and satellite observations of nitrogen dioxide (NO2), a traffic-related pollutant, to measure the air quality and equity effects of the growing e-commerce and warehousing industries in the United States. Coverage: nearly 150,000 warehouses across the country. Warehouses worsen local traffic-related air pollution, with an average near-warehouse NO2 enhancement of nearly 20%, and are disproportionately located in marginalised and minoritised communities; near-warehouse truck traffic and NO2 increase significantly with warehouse density and with the number of loading docks and parking spaces. The authors point to indirect source rules, incentives to replace old trucks and corporate electrification commitments. Format and access: an open access article. Licence and cost: free under CC BY 4.0. Caveats: satellite NO2 is a column measure at coarse resolution, so single facilities need ground monitoring. The exposure relationships can be used to add health and equity burdens to freight facility siting and truck routing models. It relates to the FHWA weather and freight assessment and the Freight Analysis Framework in the catalogue.
